name: Kosovo
summary_text: Article 24 of the Constitution of the Republic of Kosovo prohibits discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation, and the 2015 Law on Protection from Discrimination extends that protection to gender identity. Outright International's March 2026 overview records that implementation of both provisions remains inconsistent in practice, so the guarantees a visitor can cite are stronger than what is reliably delivered.  Legal gender recognition runs through the courts rather than an administrative procedure. In January 2019 Blert Morina's application for a name and gender-marker change on Kosovo identity documents was before the Constitutional Court of Kosovo, and applicants in Kosovo followed closely the European Court of Human Rights ruling in X v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, which held that a surgical requirement for changing a gender marker violates private-life rights.  Partner recognition remains unadopted law. Parliament rejected a law recognising same-sex civil unions in March 2022. Prime Minister Albin Kurti pledged in April 2024 to legalise same-sex civil unions, and a Justice Ministry working group was drafting the relevant bill, but as of February 2026 Parliament had still not adopted the new Civil Code amid fierce opposition that included the ruling party. IntelliNews reports that the draft Civil Code's gender-neutral marriage language would open the way to same-sex marriage if it enters into force.  Public LGBTI organising is visible in Prishtina, where the third annual Pride Parade was held alongside a week of exhibitions, conferences and discussions organised by the Center for Equality and Liberty. The CSGD annual report for 2022 documented intolerance and hatred, with hate speech by politicians common during the Civil Code debates, and an artist received death threats over a painting.

sources.title: Criminal Code of Kosovo - April 2019 version
sources.documents: Provides stronger protections and additional penalties for hate crime motivated by victim's sexual orientation or gender identity; enforcement context includes 10 bias crimes reported to authorities in 2019, 13 to NGOs, and Feb 2019 case against Ministry of Justice official calling for beheading LGBTQ people
sources.detail: Cited as 'new Criminal Code of Kosovo went into force' in April 2019. No URL visible.

name: Zimbabwe
summary_text: Zimbabwe criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. The offence covers sodomy and, per the Human Dignity Trust country profile, acts involving contact between males that would be regarded by a reasonable person as indecent, so conduct short of intercourse can still fall within the criminal law.  Amnesty International's report of 9 January 2024 (index AFR 01/7533/2024), 'We are facing extinction — escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment, the weaponisation of law and their human rights implications in select African countries', examines rising anti-LGBTI sentiment and the use of law against LGBTI people in the countries it covers, Zimbabwe among them. The report's finding of law being deployed as an instrument of hostility is the operative risk context for a visitor, alongside the statutory exposure itself.  Healthcare access is formally protected. In July 2018 the Zimbabwean health ministry released a 68-page training handbook for all health practitioners on serving gay people, sex workers and transgender or non-gender-conforming people in public health institutions. The manual states that care for these groups is legal and every provider's duty, recording that nowhere in policy or law states it is illegal to provide healthcare services to members of key population groups. It was issued because patients had avoided clinics fearing mistreatment or police tip-offs by staff. For a trans visitor this means formal policy guarantees health-service access, including transition-relevant care at public facilities, though day-to-day treatment depends on staff trained under a 2018 handbook.  GALZ (Gays and Lesbians of Zimbabwe), a voluntary membership organisation established in 1990 with more than 4,000 community members, 35 years of advocacy, 10 affinity groups and 4 resource centres, provides legal support explicitly covering arrests for 'sodomy', counselling, hospital-fee assistance and empowerment programmes for LGBTI Zimbabweans. Legal aid and counselling remain reachable for an LGBTI traveller despite criminalisation.

sources.title: Zimbabwe Criminal Code - sodomy / unlawful sexual conduct provisions
sources.documents: Defines sodomy as anal sexual intercourse or any 'indecent act' between consenting adults; basis for criminalization of same-sex sexual activity.
